title: India-US trade portal reaches about 3,500 registrations in six months
subtitle: A free online market built by India's consulates in the US helps small Indian firms meet American buyers, and Piyush Goyal calls the response encouraging.
content_html:
About 3,500 registrations in a few months. That is how many sign-ups a free online market linking Indian sellers with American buyers has picked up so far. Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal shared the figure in a post on X, as The Economic Times reported on 27 October 2026. He called the response "encouraging".

The platform is called the India-US Trade Facilitation Portal. Here is what the portal does, who made it, and why small Indian firms are the ones it is really built for.

So what is this portal, in plain words?

Think of a matrimonial app, but for companies. On one side, Indian exporters put up their products. On the other side, buyers in the US look around and pick the sellers they like.

An exporter is simply a seller who sends goods or services to another country. If a spice maker in Kerala ships pepper to a shop in New Jersey, the spice maker is an exporter.

The ET report calls the portal a digital B2B marketplace. B2B means "business to business". Picture a samosa stall owner buying a big sack of potatoes from a wholesaler. Nobody here is buying one samosa for themselves. One business is selling to another business, usually in bulk.

The portal was built by the Consulate General of India in New York, together with other Indian consulates in the US and India's top diplomatic office in Washington DC. A consulate is like a branch office of a country's government in a foreign city. A circular from the Plastics Export Promotion Council names the other cities in the team: Chicago, Los Angeles, Atlanta, Boston, Houston, Seattle and San Francisco.

Who launched it, and when?

Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri, along with Vinay Kwatra, India's top envoy in the US, launched the portal at a virtual event. The date was 8 April 2026. So from launch to the 3,500 figure is a little over six months.

Goyal joined the launch by video. He described the portal as "the runway to the United States of America", according to a PTI report carried by DT Next. Here is his full launch message.

On launch day he also posted about the portal on X.

Misri made an interesting point at the launch. He said several B2B platforms already exist, but a platform made only for India and the US can unlock the full potential of this partnership, Orissa POST reported. He also said governments are now stepping in as matchmakers, connecting buyers and sellers.

What can a seller actually do on it?

According to the ET report, the portal has:

  • Product listings by category, so a buyer looking for, say, handicrafts does not have to scroll through car parts.
  • A search tool for buyers to find what they want.
  • Personal dashboards where users can track business leads and sales. A lead is a possible customer who showed interest, like a person at your stall asking the price twice.
  • Virtual exhibitions and curated showcases, which are like online trade fairs where firms show off their products.

Registration is free, the plastics council's circular says. An earlier circular lists the sign-up steps on the portal's registration page. An exporter picks the "Exporter" option and enters its IEC code with the certificate. Next, the firm uploads papers like GST, PAN and its certificate of incorporation. Then the export promotion council the firm belongs to checks the membership and approves the profile. After that, the exporter logs in with two-step security, the same kind of extra check a bank app uses.

Why are small firms the main target?

In his X post, Goyal said the portal will open up new chances for Indian businesses, "particularly MSMEs & first-time exporters", the ET report says.

MSME stands for micro, small and medium enterprises. These are the little engines of India's economy: a family pickle unit, a small garment workshop, a tiny software team working out of a rented flat. A first-time exporter is a firm that has only ever sold inside India and now wants to try a foreign market.

For such firms, finding a buyer abroad is hard. A big company can fly people to the US for trade fairs. A small firm usually cannot. So it often depends on middlemen, people who connect the seller and the buyer and keep a share of the money. One summary of the portal, by Chronicle India, says the portal reduces intermediaries. That is the formal word for middlemen.

At the launch, Goyal said the portal would give chances to many kinds of people, from a farmer in Punjab and a jeweller in Surat to a software expert in Bengaluru and pharma firms in Telangana, Orissa POST reported.

The New York consulate is also running online sessions for exporters. It planned a webinar with Walmart on 29 May on how Indian products can reach US shelves, DT Next reported. Before that, India's consulate in Seattle held a similar session with Costco, and over 200 Indian exporters joined.

The bigger goal: Mission 500

This portal is one small part of a much larger plan. Speaking at the launch, Misri said India-US trade reached a record 241 billion US dollars in the last year, All India Radio News reported. That was 15 percent growth. It was also the fourth year in a row the US was India's largest trading partner.

Both countries want to take this to 500 billion dollars by 2030. They call the target Mission 500. That is a little more than double the present level. Imagine your cricket team scored 241 runs last season and now the captain wants 500. Every player has to chip in, including the tail-enders. Small exporters are the tail-enders here.

There is also a trade deal in the works. On 26 October 2026, at a business event with the Netherlands, Goyal said, "We have concluded most of the discussions and are fine-tuning the agreement", ET reported. The deal is not final yet. Tariffs are the big question. A tariff is a tax a country charges on goods coming in from abroad, a bit like an entry fee at a fair. Since then, the US has put an extra 10% duty on Indian goods under a probe called Section 301, the same ET report says.

What does 3,500 really tell us?

It tells us that a good number of firms are curious. Signing up is free and only takes some papers, so interest is easy to show. The reports do not say how many of these sign-ups are Indian sellers and how many are US buyers. They also do not say how many actual orders have come through the portal yet.

So think of 3,500 as the number of people who walked into a new mall in its first six months. It is a good start. The real test is how many of them leave with a shopping bag. That will show up only when the portal starts sharing deal numbers.

Why should a young reader care?

Many young Indians grow up around a family business, or dream of starting one. A handloom unit, a spice brand, a small app studio. A free government portal makes the first step towards a buyer in America a little easier. It does not promise orders. Still, the portal gives a small firm a seat at the same table as bigger ones.
